messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kwame's Vigilance

Kwame was sixty-five years old when Hurricane Helene made landfall near his home in coastal North Carolina. He had worked retail for forty-two years—first as a stock clerk, then as a floor supervisor at a large electronics store in Wilmington—and he prided himself on his reliability. On the morning of the hurricane, he had driven his wife Ama to her sister's house inland, then returned alone to secure the store. The wind was already fierce, the sky a sickly green-grey. He was checking the loading dock doors when the wall of the building adjacent to theirs collapsed. The sound was immense, a roar and a crack, and Kwame felt the shock wave push him backward. He watched through the store windows as debris—wood, metal, a section of corrugated roof—spiraled through the air. For several seconds he stood frozen, watching the chaos unfold with the terrible clarity of someone who knows he might die in the next moment. Then he ran.

He made it to his car and drove to Ama's sister's house with his hands shaking. The store was damaged but repairable. Kwame was not. In the weeks that followed, he returned to work—the store reopened after three weeks—but something had fundamentally shifted in how he moved through the world. What had struck him most viscerally during those seconds at the loading dock was his complete powerlessness. The building could fail. The sky could fall. There was no warning that mattered, no way to predict or prevent catastrophe. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was an illusion he had been foolish enough to trust. This conviction—that he could be destroyed at any moment by forces beyond his control—shaped everything that followed.

Because Kwame was certain the world remained perilously unsafe, he began to take precautions. He arrived at the store each morning and immediately scanned the ceiling, the walls, the structural supports. He positioned himself near the exit whenever possible, a habit so ingrained that he no longer consciously chose it; his body simply gravitated toward the door. When he walked through the stockroom, he noted the fire exits. When he sat in the break room, he mentally mapped the quickest route out. He found himself constantly scanning the environment for signs of threat—a crack in the plaster, a wobble in a shelf, the way the fluorescent lights hummed. These vigilant routines felt necessary, even protective. They were his answer to the conviction that disaster could strike without warning. If he stayed alert, if he stayed near the exit, perhaps he could escape the next time.

But Kwame's hypervigilance came at a cost. His sleep deteriorated almost immediately. He would lie awake beside Ama, his body tense, his mind unable to settle. He had come to believe that he needed to stay alert even at night, that lowering his guard was dangerous. His difficulty falling asleep was not simple insomnia; it was the biological expression of his certainty that danger lurked. The more he stayed awake, scanning the darkness of their bedroom for threats, the more convinced he became that his vigilance was justified—that something terrible would happen if he allowed himself to truly rest.

His memories of those seconds at the loading dock had taken on a peculiar quality. When they surfaced—and they surfaced constantly, unbidden, during quiet moments at work or in the car—they felt not like memories but like present reality. The sound of the collapse would replay in his mind like a film stuck on a loop, and in those moments, Kwame was not remembering the hurricane; he was back there, feeling the shock wave, watching debris spiral. The memory felt as immediate and dangerous as the original event. And because the memory felt present, not past, his body responded as if the threat were current. His heart would race. His breathing would shallow. This physiological arousal, in turn, seemed to confirm that danger was real and imminent, which intensified his conviction that he had to remain vigilant, that the world was as dangerous as he feared. Each time the memory replayed and his body reacted, it reinforced his belief that permanent damage had been done to him—that he could no longer trust his own safety, his own sense of security.

The scanning, the positioning near exits, the constant environmental checking—these strategies gave Kwame a fragile sense of control. But they also kept him trapped. The more he scanned, the more threats he seemed to find. The more he stayed near the exit, the more his nervous system remained primed for escape. His coworkers had begun to notice his restlessness, his refusal to work in the back stockroom for more than a few minutes at a time. His supervisor had asked if he was feeling alright. Kwame could not explain that he was no longer the man they had known, that something fundamental in him had fractured and could not be repaired. He was sixty-five years old, and he was afraid of his own workplace. He was afraid of buildings. He was afraid of the sky. He was afraid that one day, without warning, the world would collapse again—and this time, no exit would save him.
